messages.content: Does the EU AI Act apply to AI systems or AI models or both?

0.answer: The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk. The Regulation therefore applies to both AI systems and general-purpose AI models under two parallel regimes.

1.answer: The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk. The Regulation therefore applies to both AI systems and general-purpose AI models under two parallel regimes.

messages.content: Under the EU AI Act, what presumption applies when a high-risk AI system is trained and tested on data that reflects the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which it is intended to be used?

1.answer: Under Article 42(1), such a system is presumed to comply with the relevant requirements of Article 10(4), which requires datasets to take into account the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting within which the high-risk AI system is intended to be used.

0.answer: Article 42(1) establishes that a high-risk AI system trained and tested on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which it is intended to be used is presumed to comply with the relevant requirements of Article 10(4), which requires datasets to take into account the characteristics or elements particular to that specific setting. This presumption is rebuttable and covers only Article 10(4); it does not extend to the broader data governance obligations in Article 10(2) and Article 10(3), which require datasets to be subject to appropriate governance practices and to be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete.

messages.content: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.

0.answer: Article 49 requires the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative to register in the EU database established by Article 71 (the Commission-managed, publicly accessible, machine-readable database for high-risk AI systems) before placing the system on the market or putting it into service. The information to be submitted is set out in Annex VIII Section A and comprises thirteen items: the name, address and contact details of the provider; where submission is carried out by another person on behalf of the provider, that person's name, address and contact details; the name, address and contact details of the authorised representative, where applicable; the AI system trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability; a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported; a basic and concise description of the information used by the system (data, inputs) and its operating logic; the status of the AI system (on the market or in service; no longer placed on the market or in service; recalled); the type, number and expiry date of the certificate issued by the notified body and the name or identification number of that notified body, where applicable; a scanned copy of that certificate, where applicable; any Member States in which the AI system has been placed on the market, put into service or made available; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47; electronic instructions for use (this item is excluded for systems in the areas of law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management under Annex III points 1, 6 and 7, which are registered in a secure non-public section under Article 49.4); and, optionally, a URL for additional information. For high-risk systems falling under Annex III points 1, 6 and 7, Article 49.4 restricts the registration to a secure non-public section and limits the submitted fields to Annex VIII Section A points 1 to 10, excluding points 6, 8 and 9, with access confined to the Commission and the designated national authorities.

1.answer: Under Annex VIII, Section A (Article 49(1)), a provider must submit: the name, address and contact details of the provider; the name, address and contact details of any person submitting on the provider's behalf; the name, address and contact details of the authorised representative where applicable; the AI system trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability; a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported; a basic and concise description of the information used by the system (data, inputs) and its operating logic; the status of the AI system; the type, number and expiry date of the certificate issued by the notified body and that body's name or identification number where applicable; a scanned copy of that certificate where applicable; any Member States in which the system has been placed on the market or put into service; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; electronic instructions for use (except for law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control systems under Annex III, points 1, 6 and 7); and, optionally, a URL for additional information.

messages.content: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?

1.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system.

0.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system.

messages.content: Under the EU AI Act, what specific information must a provider/prospective provider submit (and keep up to date) regarding testing of a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside an AI regulatory sandbox?

0.answer: Under Article 60, a provider or prospective provider must draw up a real-world testing plan and submit it to the market surveillance authority in the Member State where testing is to be conducted, which governs testing of high-risk AI systems in real world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes. The provider must also register the testing in the EU database with a Union-wide unique single identification number and the information specified in Annex IX, except that systems falling under Annex III points 1, 6, and 7 (law enforcement, migration, asylum, and border control) register instead in the secure non-public section under Article 49(4), and systems under Annex III point 2 register under Article 49(5). During testing, the provider must report any serious incident to the national market surveillance authority under Article 73, adopt immediate mitigation measures or suspend testing, and notify the authority of any suspension, termination, and the final outcomes. The provider must keep all of this information current, as Article 60 requires notification of changes in status and final results, and the Commission is empowered to specify the detailed elements of the real-world testing plan by implementing acts.

1.answer: Under Article 60(4), a provider or prospective provider must draw up a real-world testing plan and submit it to the market surveillance authority (Article 60(4)(a)), obtain that authority's approval (Article 60(4)(b)), and register the testing in the EU database with a Union-wide unique single identification number and the information specified in Annex IX (or, for law-enforcement/migration/asylum/border-control systems under Annex III points 1, 6 and 7, in the secure non-public section) (Article 60(4)(c)). The provider must also notify the authority of any suspension or termination and of the final outcomes (Article 60(8)), and report any serious incident to the authority (Article 60(7)). The Commission will specify the detailed elements of the real-world testing plan by implementing acts (Article 60(1)).

messages.content: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, what is the definition of (a) a "conformity assessment body" and (b) "conformity assessment"?

1.answer: Under Article 3(21), a conformity assessment body means a body that performs third-party conformity assessment activities, including testing, certification and inspection. Under Article 3(20), conformity assessment means the process of demonstrating whether the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 relating to a high-risk AI system have been fulfilled.

0.answer: Article 3.20 defines "conformity assessment" as the process of demonstrating whether the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 relating to a high-risk AI system have been fulfilled. Article 3.21 defines "conformity assessment body" as a body that performs third-party conformity assessment activities, including testing, certification and inspection. A conformity assessment body that is notified in accordance with the Regulation and other relevant Union harmonisation legislation becomes a "notified body" within the meaning of Article 3.22.

messages.content: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.

0.answer: Article 17(1) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to document a quality management system in written policies, procedures and instructions covering at least thirteen elements: a strategy for regulatory compliance including conformity assessment procedures and management of modifications; techniques and procedures for design, design control and design verification; techniques and procedures for development, quality control and quality assurance; examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency; technical specifications including standards and means to ensure compliance where harmonised standards are not fully applied; systems and procedures for data management covering data acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, retention and any other data operation performed before and for the purpose of placing on the market; the risk management system referred to in Article 9; the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system in accordance with Article 72, which requires providers to establish, document and actively operate a system that collects, documents and analyses relevant data throughout the system's lifetime; procedures related to the reporting of a serious incident in accordance with Article 73; handling of communication with national competent authorities, notified bodies, other operators and interested parties; systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information; resource management including security-of-supply measures; and an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of management and other staff for all aspects listed. Article 17(2) provides that implementation shall be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation, while Article 17(3) allows providers already subject to sectoral Union law quality management obligations to integrate these elements into those existing systems, and Article 17(4) provides that financial institutions subject to Union financial services law internal governance requirements are deemed to fulfil the quality management system obligation by complying with those rules, except for the risk management system, post-market monitoring, and serious incident reporting elements of Article 17(1)(g), (h) and (i), which remain mandatory in all cases.

1.answer: Under Article 17(1), the QMS must be documented in written policies, procedures and instructions and include at least: a regulatory compliance strategy (including conformity assessment and modification management); design, design control and design verification techniques and procedures; development, quality control and quality assurance techniques and procedures; examination, test and validation procedures with their frequency; applicable technical specifications and standards, with means to ensure compliance where harmonised standards are not fully applied; data management systems and procedures covering acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, retention and all related operations; the risk management system; the post-market monitoring system; serious incident reporting procedures; communication handling with competent authorities, notified bodies, other operators and interested parties; record-keeping systems and procedures; resource management including security-of-supply measures; and an accountability framework setting out management and staff responsibilities for all the foregoing aspects.

messages.content: Under the EU AI Act, what is the scientific panel of independent experts, what are its main support/advisory tasks, and what key characteristics/selection requirements apply to its members?

1.answer: Under Article 68, the scientific panel is a body of independent experts established by the Commission via implementing act to support enforcement of the Regulation. Its main advisory/support tasks are: alerting the AI Office of possible systemic risks of GPAI models (Article 90); contributing to tools and methodologies for evaluating GPAI capabilities, including benchmarks; advising on classification of GPAI models with systemic risk; advising on classification of various GPAI models and systems; contributing to development of tools and templates; supporting market surveillance authorities on request; supporting cross-border market surveillance (Article 74(11)); and supporting the AI Office in Union safeguard procedures (Article 81). Members must have up-to-date scientific or technical AI expertise, be independent from any AI provider, and be able to act diligently, accurately and objectively; they must perform tasks impartially, maintain confidentiality, take no instructions from anyone, and each draw up a publicly available declaration of interests.

0.answer: Article 68 establishes the scientific panel of independent experts, created by the Commission through an implementing act, to support enforcement of the GPAI provisions by performing five tasks: alerting the AI Office to possible systemic risks of general-purpose AI models at Union level in accordance with Article 90, contributing to the development of tools and methodologies for evaluating capabilities of general-purpose AI models and systems including through benchmarks, providing advice on the classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, providing advice on the classification of various general-purpose AI models and systems more broadly, and contributing to the development of tools and templates. As to member characteristics, Article 68 requires that experts perform their tasks with impartiality and objectivity, ensure confidentiality of information and data obtained in carrying out their tasks, neither seek nor take instructions from anyone when exercising their panel functions, and each draw up a declaration of interests that is made publicly available, with the AI Office establishing systems and procedures to actively manage and prevent potential conflicts of interest.

messages.content: Under the EU AI Act, if a provider identifies a serious incident during testing in real-world conditions of a high-risk AI system, what three actions must the provider take?

0.answer: When a serious incident is identified during testing in real-world conditions of a high-risk AI system, Article 60.7 requires the provider to take three actions: first, report the serious incident to the national market surveillance authority in accordance with Article 73, which requires providers to notify the market surveillance authority of the Member State where the incident occurred within the tiered deadlines set by Article 73 (immediately for widespread infringement or critical-infrastructure disruption and no later than two days after awareness, no later than ten days for death, and no later than fifteen days for other serious incidents). Second, the provider must adopt immediate mitigation measures or, failing that, suspend the testing in real-world conditions until such mitigation takes place, or otherwise terminate it. Third, the provider must establish a procedure for the prompt recall of the AI system upon termination of the testing in real-world conditions, where Article 3.16 defines recall as any measure aiming to achieve the return to the provider or taking out of service or disabling the use of an AI system made available to deployers.

1.answer: Under Article 60(7), a provider that identifies a serious incident during real-world testing outside a sandbox must: (1) report the incident to the national market surveillance authority in accordance with Article 73; (2) adopt immediate mitigation measures or, failing that, suspend the testing until such mitigation takes place, or otherwise terminate it; and (3) establish a procedure for the prompt recall of the AI system upon such termination of the testing in real-world conditions.

messages.content: What must a distributor do if it considers a high-risk AI system is not in conformity with the Act's requirements? Additionally, what extra steps are required if the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1)?

1.answer: Under Article 24(2), where a distributor considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system is not in conformity with the requirements of Section 2, it shall not make the system available on the market until it has been brought into conformity. Additionally, where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), the distributor shall inform the provider or the importer, as applicable, to that effect. Where the non-conformity concerns a system already made available on the market, Article 24(4) requires the distributor to take corrective actions to bring the system into conformity, withdraw it, or recall it, or ensure the provider, importer, or relevant operator does so; if an Article 79(1) risk is present, the distributor shall immediately inform the provider or importer and the competent authorities, giving details of the non-compliance and any corrective actions taken.

0.answer: Under Article 24(2), a distributor that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system is not in conformity with the Section 2 requirements must not make the system available on the market until it has been brought into conformity. Where the non-conforming system also presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), Article 24(2) additionally requires the distributor to inform the provider or the importer, as applicable, to that effect. If the non-conformity is discovered after the system has already been made available on the market, Article 24(4) requires the distributor to take the corrective actions necessary to bring the system into conformity, to withdraw it, or to recall it, or to ensure that the provider, the importer, or any relevant operator takes those corrective actions. Where that already-distributed system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), Article 24(4) further requires the distributor to immediately inform both the provider or importer and the competent authorities for the high-risk AI system concerned, giving details of the non-compliance and of any corrective actions taken.

messages.content: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?

0.answer: Using an AI-equipped drone to identify who is present in a public area constitutes real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces, which is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h) when carried out by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, subject only to the three narrow exceptions in Article 5(1)(h)(i)-(iii): a targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, or sexual exploitation or for missing persons; prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or of a terrorist attack; or localisation of a suspect of a serious Annex II offence. Where the same drone-based identification is operated by a private actor for non-law-enforcement purposes, it is not prohibited under Article 5(1)(h), but it may be high-risk under Article 6(2) via Annex III depending on the specific use case, or it may trigger the Article 50 transparency obligation where the system interacts directly with natural persons. A toy drone is not exempt from the Act's substantive rules by virtue of being a toy: if the AI system embedded in it performs a prohibited practice, the prohibition applies regardless of the platform, though a toy drone whose AI performs only minimal functions such as obstacle avoidance with no biometric identification or categorisation is minimal risk with no mandatory obligations. If a toy drone's AI system is itself a product or a safety component of a product covered by the Toy Safety Directive listed in Annex I and that product requires third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, the AI system is high-risk under Article 6(1), which classifies AI systems as high-risk where they are a safety component of, or themselves, a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation that undergoes third-party conformity assessment.

1.answer: Using AI in a drone to identify persons in public ("find who's around in town") likely constitutes real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces, which is prohibited for law enforcement under Article 5(1)(h) and classified as high-risk under Annex III(1)(a). For non-law-enforcement private use, it remains high-risk under Annex III(1)(a) and may trigger prohibitions under Article 5(1)(e)-(g) depending on the specific function (facial database scraping, biometric categorisation, emotion recognition). A toy drone falls under Directive 2009/48/EC (Annex I, item 2); if the AI system is a safety component or the product itself and requires third-party conformity assessment, it is high-risk under Article 6(1). For other applications on a toy drone, the same Article 6(1) route applies, and if the AI additionally falls within Annex III categories, Article 6(2) applies independently.

messages.content: Article 9 of the AI Act lists the five categories of harm that map to AI systems with: no risk, limited risk, high-risk, systemic risk, prohibited. What are the five categories and how do they map to the five risk levels?

1.answer: Article 9 does not establish five risk categories or map them to risk levels. Article 9 exclusively governs the risk management system for high-risk AI systems, requiring identification and analysis of known and foreseeable risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights; estimation and evaluation of risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluation of post-market monitoring data; and adoption of targeted risk management measures. The five-tier risk structure (prohibited, high-risk, limited-risk, minimal/no risk, and systemic risk for GPAI models) derives from Articles 5, 6, 50, and 51 respectively, not from Article 9.

0.answer: Article 9 does not establish the five risk categories or map AI systems to risk levels; that premise is incorrect. The EU AI Act's risk framework is structured across multiple provisions, not Article 9, which governs only the risk management system that providers of high-risk AI systems must establish, implement, document, and maintain across the lifecycle. The four risk tiers are: prohibited practices under Article 5 (subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, criminal risk profiling based solely on personality traits, untargeted facial image scraping, emotion recognition in workplaces or educational institutions, biometric categorisation inferring race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement); high-risk under Article 6, either as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment, or as a system falling within the Annex III use cases; limited risk under Article 50, which imposes transparency duties such as disclosing AI interaction to natural persons; and minimal risk, which carries no mandatory obligations under the Act. In parallel, the Act establishes a separate regime for general-purpose AI models under Articles 51 to 56, where Article 51 classifies a model as having systemic risk when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs or the Commission so designates it under Annex XIII criteria, triggering the additional obligations in Article 55 including adversarial testing, systemic risk mitigation, serious incident reporting, and cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure.

messages.content: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?

0.answer: No, the deployer cannot simply proceed with the new use without first assessing whether it triggers a role change under Article 25, which provides that a deployer who modifies the intended purpose of a high-risk AI system becomes a provider and assumes all provider obligations. Even if the legal team's assessment that neither Annex I nor Annex III applies to the new use is correct, that self-assessment must be documented before the system is put to the new use, and the deployer-turned-provider would need to verify that the modification does not constitute a substantial modification that re-triggers the original high-risk classification under Article 6. On logging, Article 26.6 requires deployers of high-risk AI systems to retain the logs automatically generated by the system, to the extent those logs are under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and in any case for at least six months, unless Union or national law provides otherwise; this obligation attaches to the system's high-risk status and continues to apply regardless of whether the specific new use falls outside Annex I and Annex III, because the system itself remains high-risk. The deployer should therefore document the intended-purpose analysis, confirm whether the Article 25 provider-transition threshold is crossed, and maintain logs for at least six months under Article 26.6 for any operation of the system during and after the transition.

1.answer: No, you cannot simply proceed without further analysis. Modifying the intended purpose of a high-risk AI system makes the operator's organisation a provider under Article 25(1), triggering full provider obligations regardless of the operator's legal team's risk assessment. Even if the new use falls outside Annex I and Annex III, that conclusion must be documented before deployment per Article 6(4). As deployer of the existing high-risk system, Article 26(6) requires the operator to retain automatically generated logs for at least six months; if the purpose change makes you a new provider, the full Chapter III Section 2 obligations apply instead. The log-retention duty under Article 26(6) attaches to the high-risk AI system as deployed, so logs must be kept regardless of whether the new use is itself high-risk.

messages.content: Can law enforcement starts using a real-time remote biometric identification system without prior authorisation? If yes, how much time do they have to seek authorisation, and what happens if the authorisation is refused?

1.answer: Yes, in a duly justified situation of urgency, law enforcement may commence use of a real-time remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces without prior authorisation, provided that authorisation is requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours (Article 5(3)). If that authorisation is refused, use shall be stopped with immediate effect and all data, results and outputs of that use shall be immediately discarded and deleted (Article 5(3)). Additionally, in urgent cases, use may commence without prior EU database registration, provided registration is completed without undue delay (Article 5(2)).

0.answer: No, not always: Article 5(1)(h), which prohibits the use of real-time remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement, contains a narrow urgency derogation in Article 46(2) that permits law enforcement authorities or civil protection authorities to put a specific high-risk AI system into service without prior authorisation in a duly justified situation of urgency for exceptional reasons of public security or in the case of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, provided that authorisation is requested during or after the use without undue delay. Article 46(2) does not fix a precise number of hours or days for that request; the statutory standard is "without undue delay", meaning as soon as practicable in the circumstances. If the authorisation is refused, Article 46(2) requires that the use of the high-risk AI system be stopped with immediate effect and that all results and outputs of such use be immediately discarded.

messages.content: If a high-risk AI system was already placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026, does the AI Act fully apply to it? What about general purpose AI systems?

0.answer: No, the AI Act does not fully apply to a high-risk AI system already on the market or in service before 2 August 2026: under Article 111(2), which establishes transitional provisions for pre-existing systems, the Regulation applies to such a system only if it undergoes a significant change in design on or after that date, meaning an unchanged legacy system is not immediately subject to the full high-risk obligation set. However, Article 111(2) also provides that providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended for use by public authorities must take the necessary steps to comply with all requirements and obligations by 2 August 2030, regardless of whether a significant design change occurs. For general-purpose AI models, Article 111(3) provides that providers of models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must take the necessary steps to comply with the obligations laid down in the Regulation, including the Article 53 duties to maintain technical documentation per Annex XI, make information available to downstream providers per Annex XII, implement a copyright compliance policy, and publish a training-data content summary, by 2 August 2027. A general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs under Article 51(2), must additionally meet the Article 55 obligations of adversarial model evaluation, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, serious incident reporting to the AI Office, and cybersecurity protection, with the same 2 August 2027 grace period applying to pre-existing models under Article 111(3).

1.answer: No, the AI Act does not fully apply to pre-existing high-risk AI systems. Under Article 111(2), the Regulation applies to high-risk AI systems placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 only if, from that date, those systems undergo significant changes in their design. Additionally, high-risk AI systems intended for use by public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030 regardless. For GPAI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025, Article 111(3) grants a transitional period: providers must take the necessary steps to comply with GPAI obligations by 2 August 2027.

messages.content: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?

1.answer: No, you cannot skip Chapter 3 Section 2. Under Article 43(3), for high-risk AI systems covered by Section A of Annex I, the requirements of Section 2 apply to the AI system and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment. Where the sectoral legal act permits opting out of third-party assessment through full application of harmonised standards, that opt-out is available under the AI Act only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards or common specifications covering all requirements set out in Section 2. The opt-out affects the procedure (no notified body), not the substantive obligations; compliance with Section 2 remains mandatory regardless.

0.answer: No, the Chapter III Section 2 requirements cannot be skipped. Article 43(3) governs conformity assessment for Annex I products and states explicitly that where the sectoral legislation permits the manufacturer to opt out of third-party conformity assessment by applying all harmonised standards, that opt-out is available under the AI Act only if the provider has also applied harmonised standards or common specifications covering all requirements set out in Chapter III Section 2. The opt-out from third-party involvement therefore does not relieve the provider of substantive compliance with Chapter III Section 2; it merely permits the conformity assessment procedure to be conducted as an internal control under Annex VI, which requires the provider to verify that the quality management system conforms to Article 17, to examine the technical documentation for compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, and to verify that the design, development process, and post-market monitoring plan are consistent with that documentation. The Chapter III Section 2 obligations remain fully applicable and must be demonstrated through that internal control procedure.
